scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Dunhuang dance is inspired by the murals and artistic heritage of the Dunhuang grottoes in the Gansu province of northwestern China.
Rooted in the imagery depicted in the cave murals of the Mogao Grottoes, the dance form draws heavily on Buddhist iconography.
It emerged as a separate classical dance form in the 1980s, following the 1979 debut of the dance drama 'Rain of Flowers Along the Silk Road' by the Gansu Dunhuang Art Academy.
on_screen: Map: China · East Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally rooted in Buddhist devotion and iconography, modern Dunhuang dance is performed in academic settings and professional shows.
It serves as a living testament to the lasting influence of Indian culture on Chinese performing arts and acts as a medium for preserving the visual history of the Silk Road.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance features unique hand movements that can be traced back to Indian classical dance forms like the Natyasastra, Bharatanatyam, and Kathakali.
It combines ethnic dance styles from Central and Western China.
Key movements include the 'S-curve' body alignment and the use of long silk scarves to simulate the flight of celestial beings.
Watch for Playing the Pipa Behind the Back, Flying Apsara.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (acHpowhdX1o)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear formations for group pieces like 'Thousand Hand Guanyin'; circular paths for soloists.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is inspired by the musical instruments and music scores found in Dunhuang.
Visual depictions in the murals show lutes (pipa), flutes, and drums, which are replicated in modern performances.
Listen for the Pipa, Dizi (flute), Drums, Zheng (zither).
The pulse is 4/4 at about 75 beats a minute.
A blend of traditional Chinese pentatonic scales with Central Asian modal influences, characterized by prominent pipa plucking and atmospheric flute melodies.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes are based on the imagery found in the Mogao Grottoes' cave paintings, often featuring high-waisted skirts and long silk ribbons.
The setting typically evokes the interior of the caves or the desert landscape of the Silk Road.
Dancers often use props like the pipa, held in unconventional positions as seen in the murals.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Zhang Jigang is a central contemporary choreographer who produced the 'Thousand Hand Guanyin' for the China Disabled Performing Art Troupe.
The Gansu Dunhuang Art Academy is credited with the 1979 production 'Rain of Flowers Along the Silk Road' which popularized the style.
The style reflects a combination of ethnic dance styles from Central and Western China, influenced by the cultural transmission across Bactria and the Tarim Basin.
The dance traces its aesthetic lineage to Indian classical traditions (Natyasastra) and historical Chinese court dances, reconstructed through the lens of 20th-century stage performance.

images.description: A dancer spins while the orchestra plays. There are three kinds of lutes in this image. The dancer has a large pipa. A smaller pipa is on the right side lower. Beside that instrument is a long-necked lute, possibly a sanxian (三弦). Mogao caves near Dunhuang―Grotto 46 Left interior wall, second panel. Also called cave 112.

images.attribution: unknown painters from Tang Dynasty / Wikimedia Commons / Public domain
images.description: Bird of Life (共命鸟), playing a pipa, with dancer playing drum. Drummer appears to be dancing the Sogdian Whirl. Middle Tang-Yulin Grotto 25 South Wall. The Jivajivaka is supposed to specifically be a two headed creature. The bird here has also been called a Kalaviṅka, and appears to be related to the Kinnara, both connected by the same Buddhist traditions.
